c.tagline: China's tropical beach capital — Hainan's palm-fringed 'Oriental Hawaii.'

taxi.fareNote: Metered fares start around ¥10; most locals hail rides or pay via Didi and mobile QR (Alipay/WeChat). Some drivers may not accept foreign cards or make change for large notes, so carry small cash.

emergency.note: 119 for fire. English-speaking operators may be limited; hotel or resort staff can help translate.

solo.f: Women's-safety index (WPS) is the main factor (68/100)

avoid.reason: Watch for seafood-restaurant overcharging and unlicensed taxis; agree prices upfront.

hood_desc: Sanya's most convenient beach district, a compact strip of sand backed by hotels, seafood restaurants, bars and shops; the easiest walkable base for first-time visitors who want the beach and nightlife on their doorstep.
A crescent of powdery white sand about 25km east of town lined with international five-star resorts and the Tropical Paradise Forest Park; the choice for a quiet, self-contained luxury beach holiday.

A long palm-fringed beach ('Coconut Dream Corridor') closest to the city, with a mix of mid-range hotels and local life; good value and sunset walks, though a wide road-fronted strip rather than a resort cove.
Sanya's newest luxury enclave, home to Atlantis, sprawling resorts and the world's largest duty-free mall; suits travelers after high-end resorts and tax-free shopping.

The workaday heart of Sanya around the Sanya River and First Market, packed with cheap seafood, street food and local shopping; best for budget travelers wanting authentic city life over resort polish.

water.note: Drink bottled or boiled water, as locals do.

transit.pay: Pay with cash, a Sanya transit card, or by scanning an Alipay/WeChat QR code; city buses cost about ¥1-2 and the tram a low flat fare. Foreign visitors can link an international card to Alipay or WeChat to pay by QR.
transit.hours: City buses run roughly 6:00 AM to 10:30 PM and the tram on similar daytime hours; there is no night service, so taxis and Didi cover late nights.
transit.note: Sanya relies on an extensive city bus network plus a single modern tram line linking the railway station toward the port; there is no metro. Resort shuttles and Didi ride-hailing fill the gaps between the beaches.

landmarks: China's showcase resort bay curves for seven kilometres of powder sand and clear water, dubbed the 'Oriental Hawaii'.
Tianya Haijiao (Edge of the Sky, Rim of the Sea)
Giant inscribed boulders on a romantic beach mark imperial China's poetic 'ends of the earth', immortalised on the old two-yuan note.
A coral islet off Haitang Bay with Hainan's clearest water, beloved for snorkelling, diving and its lush walking trails.
A hilltop statue retells the Li legend of a deer transforming into a maiden, with Sanya's best sweeping city-and-bay night views.
Sanya's most accessible crescent bay, buzzing day and night with swimmers, seafood restaurants and a palm-lined promenade.
Hanging bridges and waterfall treks thread through steamy tropical rainforest in the mountains an hour north of the city.
A quick ferry reaches this fishing island of coral coves, sea-view cliffs and water sports in Sanya Bay's turquoise waters.
Five futuristic bulbous towers on a man-made islet light up in synchronised LED displays, defining Sanya's harbour skyline after dark.
A twenty-kilometre coconut-palm promenade tracing the city's home bay, famous for fiery sunsets over the South China Sea.

train.note: Sanya has no international trains. It is the southern terminus of Hainan's high-speed ring railway, with services running up the east coast to Haikou in about 1.5-2 hours at speeds of up to 250 km/h and round the quieter west coast as well. Long-distance conventional trains also come through, reaching the island via the Guangdong-Hainan train ferry across the Qiongzhou Strait: Guangzhou takes about 15 hours, Beijing around 35 hours and Shanghai about 36 hours, which makes the carriages-on-a-boat crossing a curiosity in itself. Three stations serve the area - Sanya Railway Station about 7 km north of downtown, plus Yalong Bay and Yazhou. Book on 12306 with your passport.

bus.note: There are no international coaches from Sanya. Two terminals operate, Sanya Bus Station on Jiefang Road and Sanya West Bus Station near the airport, and the busiest route is the hourly service to and from Haikou East Bus Station, a 3.5-hour ride for about ¥50. Buses also serve the resort bays, Lingshui and the inland towns of Wuzhishan and Baoting that the railway does not reach. Tickets are bought at the counter on the day.

ferry.note: Despite being a major coastal resort, Sanya has no scheduled passenger ferry route - Hainan's sea crossings all run from Haikou at the other end of the island, where boats cross the Qiongzhou Strait to Hai'an and Xuwen in Guangdong in roughly 1-2 hours. What Sanya does have is the Phoenix Island International Cruise Terminal, from which cruise ships depart, including sailings to the Paracel Islands of around 64 hours round trip for about ¥4,000 that are sold only to Chinese nationals.

half.blurb: A peninsula reserve in Lingshui county home to a large troop of free-ranging macaques, reached by cable car over a lagoon.

half.name: Nanshan Guanyin (Nanshan Cultural Tourism Zone)
half.blurb: A 108-metre triple-faced Guanyin statue rises from the sea beside Nanshan Temple, among the tallest religious statues on Earth.

full.name: Xinglong
full.blurb: An overseas-Chinese resettlement town known for a tropical botanical garden, coffee plantations, and hot-spring resorts.

full.name: Wuzhishan
full.blurb: Hainan's highest peak, a forested mountain popular for hiking, near Li and Miao minority settlements in the island's interior.
